name: Tara Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a small agency in a market town, eight of us in a converted grain store. Most of our clients are farm suppliers, feed merchants, tractor dealers, builders, so I do a lot of product catalogues, van livery and stands for the county show. A normal day is laying out sixty pages of seed prices and making sure every photo matches the right code, which is fiddly but I'm good at it. What I like is seeing our stand at the show in July. What wears me out is late price changes the night before print.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about home and money.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Rhys, my partner. He's an electrician, self-employed, and we got a small terraced house last year with help from both our families on the deposit. We've got about ten months saved on top of that, because Rhys's work goes up and down and we like a buffer. We'd like to get married and have children in the next few years. At work I use AI now and then, mainly to tidy product descriptions, once I saw the others using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. Our clients aren't exactly racing to change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful helper for boring bits, like product blurbs, and that's it. At Sunday lunch with Rhys's family, I'd say the farmers were right not to get excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased. Gwen, who owns the agency, has kept the same clients for fifteen years, and they pay on time. If AI only shaves a bit off the catalogue work, my job's steady and we can stick to our plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am, maybe use the description tool a bit more so I can leave on time. We'd book the wedding for the spring after next and keep the savings where they are. I'd also ask Gwen if I could take on the county show stand design myself this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the boring version, and boring suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rhys's work. He had six slow weeks last winter and that's when we lean on my wage. If farm incomes have a bad year, our clients cut their catalogues too, so my partner Rhys and I would both feel it at once. But we've got the buffer for exactly that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the agency would feel the small changes most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Dave, who writes our product copy. If the tool does the descriptions, Gwen might give his writing to me and keep him on just photography. Dave's been there longer than me, so I'd feel awkward.

say: AI is a **useful helper** for boring bits like product blurbs.
The farmers were right not to get **excited**, she'd tell Rhys's family.
think: Gwen's **long-standing clients** pay on time and keep her job steady.
AI shaving catalogue work leaves the **wedding and family** plan as it is.
do: Use the **description tool** more so she can leave on time.
Book the **wedding** for the spring after next.
Ask Gwen to let her design the **county show stand**.
feel: **Calm**, because the boring version suits her.
S0.quote: If farm incomes have a bad year, our clients cut their catalogues too, so my partner Rhys and I would both feel it at once.
fieldNote: Her **background risk** is farm incomes and Rhys's uneven work, not AI.
She'd take over **Dave's writing**, and feels awkward about it.
The **buffer** of ten months makes her calm here.

steps.text: Take on the county show stand design for Gwen this year
Use the description tool for catalogue product blurbs
Book the wedding with Rhys for the spring after next

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more real. Catalogues are basically planning and checking, so I can see where that goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people still want to deal with someone they know, especially round here. If someone posted that designers were finished, I'd probably reply that the feed merchant still rings Gwen, not a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a lot of my catalogue work is exactly what the card says: checking prices, planning pages. If software does the layout from a price list, Gwen needs fewer of us. I don't think she'd let me go, but I could see my hours cut to four days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the catalogue tools properly once a couple of the other agencies had tried them, so I'm the one who runs them at Gwen's. I'd move more into the show stands and van livery, which need someone measuring real vans. We'd keep the wedding but make it smaller, and put an extra hundred a month into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not scared, but it would be on my mind driving to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't think Gwen would let you go. Why so sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my boss Gwen is old-fashioned in a good way, and she'd rather keep people than chase every penny. She hired me from the local college and she's said that more than once. But four days instead of five, I could see that, and I'd accept it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up if your hours went to four days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second car, probably. Rhys has the van, and I could get the bus to the grain store most days. And we'd do the honeymoon somewhere close instead of abroad.

say: People still want to deal with **someone they know**.
The **feed merchant** still rings Gwen, not a computer.
think: Her catalogue work is the **planning and checking** the card names.
She could see her hours cut to **four days**.
do: Learn the **catalogue tools** once other agencies have tried them.
Move into **show stands** and van livery, which need real measuring.
Add **a hundred a month** to savings and shrink the wedding.
feel: **A bit uneasy**, on her mind driving to work.
S1.quote: My boss Gwen is old-fashioned in a good way, and she'd rather keep people than chase every penny.
fieldNote: She expects **fewer hours**, which makes this anxious though she sounds calm.
Her trust in **Gwen's loyalty** softens the blow.
She'd move toward work that needs **real measuring**, like van livery.

steps.text: Learn the catalogue layout tools once other agencies use them
Add an extra hundred a month to savings
Sell the second car and take the bus to work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before we'd even planned the wedding properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities need to look after each other, because the government won't be ready. I'd probably say at church that we should keep an eye on the young ones just starting out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job's gone by 2028. Catalogues, livery, stands, it's all screen work at the design stage. Rhys's work is hands-on, so he has until about 2031, and that matters a lot, because he'd be the one earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, we'd bring the wedding forward and do it small, this summer, at the village hall. I'd start helping Rhys with his business, quotes and booking, while I still have a wage, though I know that's thinking work too. And I'd think hard about having our first baby sooner, while we've still got savings and his income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A bit sick, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why have a baby sooner, rather than wait to see what happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because waiting doesn't make it better in that picture. If I'm going to lose my job anyway, I'd rather be at home with a baby while my partner Rhys is still earning. I don't want to be job-hunting in 2031 when the robots come for his work too. My mum did the same in the last recession.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I can't picture. We'd have the house and some savings, and both our families are close. I don't want handouts, but I suppose I'd take whatever's going if it came to that.

say: Families and communities need to **look after each other**.
At church she'd say to **watch the young ones** starting out.
think: Her **design job** is gone by 2028, since it's all screen work.
Rhys's **hands-on work** lasts until about 2031, making him the earner.
do: Bring the **wedding forward** to this summer at the village hall.
Help with **Rhys's quotes** and bookings while she still has a wage.
Have a **first baby sooner** while savings and Rhys's income hold.
S2.quote: If I'm going to lose my job anyway, I'd rather be at home with a baby while my partner Rhys is still earning.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job**, so this is clearly alarmed.
The robots' **three-year lag** for Rhys's trade shapes the whole family plan.
She'd reluctantly take **state help** after 2031, despite disliking handouts.

steps.text: Hold a small wedding at the village hall this summer
Leave the agency to have a baby while Rhys still earns
Rely on both families nearby for help and childcare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better. Still fast, but I could do something with five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready, and that young people should think about trades. Round here a lot of my school friends went into farming and building, and I'd say they were the sensible ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job goes around 2031. But five years means I could get married, have one baby, and come back to work for a bit before it ends. And Rhys gets until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep working and learn the new tools once the others do. We'd marry next spring as planned and try for a baby the year after. Over the five years, I'd learn to build the show stands, not just draw them, working with the carpenter Gwen uses, because that's hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. We'd have a plan and some time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really go into building stands? That's a big change.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've watched Pete the carpenter put our show stand together every July. It's measuring, cutting, fitting graphics on the panels, and I'm good with my hands. If my screen work goes, building stands is the closest thing to what I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rhys say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rhys would say we'll manage, like he always does. He'd probably want me to do his books, but that's the kind of thing AI takes anyway. I'd rather learn something that lasts.

say: Young people should think about **trades**, like her school friends in farming and building.
think: Five years allows a **wedding and one baby** before it ends, and Rhys has until 2034.
do: Learn the **new tools** once colleagues have.
Marry next spring and **try for a baby** the year after.
Learn to **build show stands** with Gwen's carpenter.
feel: **Anxious** but steady, with a plan and time.
S3.quote: If my screen work goes, building stands is the closest thing to what I do now.
fieldNote: She picks a **hands-on next step** close to her current work.
She **rejects doing Rhys's books**, seeing it as AI-exposed.
She still expects her job to end, so mood stays **anxious**.

steps.text: Learn to build county show stands with Pete the carpenter
Marry Rhys next spring and try for a baby the year after
Pick up the catalogue AI tools once colleagues have them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time in a small town. People retire, kids grow up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to get it right, and that schools should push apprenticeships now. I'd probably say it at the school gate once we've got kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it means I have the normal life I planned for most of a decade: wedding, kids, house. My job ends around 2036, but by then I'd want to be part-time anyway with young children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, nothing big. Marry, have our children, keep saving. Around 2030 I'd start learning the stand building, and I'd only use AI more when everyone else at the agency did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. Mostly fine, with a thought at the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn something with their hands and something with their heads, and not to put all their eggs in one basket. That's what my grandad said about the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years make you more relaxed or more likely to put it off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put it off, honestly. I'm not someone who changes before I have to. But we've got savings and a house, so putting it off isn't reckless for us.

say: There's **time** to get it right if people start planning now.
Schools should push **apprenticeships** now, she'd say at the school gate.
think: She gets the **normal life** she planned for most of a decade.
Her job ends around **2036**, when she'd want part-time anyway.
do: Use AI more only once **everyone else** at the agency does.
S4.quote: I'd tell my children to learn something with their hands and something with their heads, and not to put all their eggs in one basket.
fieldNote: Her job is **safe for years**, so the mood is uneasy.
She openly admits she'd **put it off**, but sees that as affordable.
Grandad's **farm advice** shapes how she'd raise her children.

steps.text: Marry Rhys and have children over the next few years
Keep ten months of expenses in savings
Wait until about 2030 before learning stand building

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It would rush the wedding and the baby and leave Rhys earning for both of us with a clock on his work too. What would help is proper apprenticeships for adults, so someone like me could learn a hands-on trade without going back to college full-time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the farmers themselves. If they can't afford catalogues, none of this matters. Our agency lives or dies on whether the feed merchants have a good year.

headlineQuote: Our agency lives or dies on whether the feed merchants have a good year.
portrait: Tara is a **27-year-old catalogue designer** at an eight-person agency serving farm suppliers in a market town.
She lives with **Rhys, a self-employed electrician**, and they have ten months saved and a new house.
Her mood tracks how soon her **screen work** ends compared with Rhys's hands-on trade.
Faster scenarios bring the **wedding and a baby** forward while Rhys still earns.
Her fallback is **building show stands** with the agency's carpenter, not doing Rhys's books.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which rushes her family plans and leaves Rhys as sole earner.
whatWouldHelp: **Adult apprenticeships** to learn a hands-on trade without full-time college.
